summary: Defines a way to split packets across several parallel PPP links, number the pieces, and put them back in order at the other end. This lets a host combine multiple slower links, such as several dial-up lines, into one larger logical connection.

eli5.summary: Imagine carrying a big pile of papers home using several small bags at once. You number the papers, so your friend can put them back in the right order when all the bags arrive.

questions: how to combine multiple ppp links
what is the endpoint discriminator in ppp
how does ppp multilink detect lost fragments
subtitle: How to split packets across several parallel PPP links, number the pieces and rebuild them in order at the far end.

tldr.problem: Systems often have several PPP links to the same peer, such as multiple ISDN channels or dial-up lines, and simply alternating packets between them can reorder the packets.
tldr.mechanism: Multilink PPP negotiates a bundle through new LCP options, then cuts packets into fragments that carry a sequence number and Beginning and Ending bits, so the receiver can put them back together in order.
tldr.outcome: Several slower links act as one larger logical link. RFC 1990 obsoletes RFC 1717 and is a Draft Standard.

today: RFC 1990 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1717, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Combine Links
sections.content:
Basic Rate and Primary Rate ISDN let a user open several simultaneous channels between two systems, buying extra bandwidth on demand. The RFC also mentions backing up a leased synchronous line with a dial-up async line at 28,800 baud, and opening additional X.25 virtual circuits where the window size is limited to two.

The simplest approach is to alternate packets between channels as space becomes available. The RFC calls this the Bank Teller's algorithm and warns that it may reorder packets. PPP Multilink (MP) instead adds a four-byte sequencing header and simple synchronization rules, so packets do not become reordered, or at least the likelihood is greatly reduced.

The method resembles the multilink protocol in ISO 7776, but it can also split and recombine packets, which reduces latency and can raise the effective maximum receive unit. It does not require acknowledged-mode operation on the link layer, though that is optionally permitted.
sections.eli5: If you have several checkout lanes open, you could send each shopper to any lane. But then the shoppers might finish in a different order than they arrived. Multilink gives everybody a number so the order can be fixed afterwards.

sections.title: Bundles and the Virtual Link
sections.content:
Each physical link first runs the normal PPP steps: LCP configures the link, and an optional Authentication phase identifies each system. Multilink then treats several such links between the same pair of systems as one aggregate link called a bundle. The bundle is named by the pair of system identifiers, and the member links can be of different kinds, for example dial-up async links paired with a leased synchronous link.

The RFC models multilink as a virtual PPP link-layer entity with its own protocol, the Multilink Protocol. Packets from all member links go to the same network-layer machinery, whether or not they carry multilink headers. Packets for network protocols sent without multilink headers cannot be sequenced and are delivered in any convenient way.

LCP negotiation is not allowed on the bundle itself. An implementation MUST NOT send LCP Configure-Request, Configure-Reject, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Terminate-Request or Terminate-Ack through the multilink procedure, and a receiver MUST silently discard them. Code-Reject, Protocol-Reject, Echo-Request, Echo-Reply and Discard-Request may be sent.

Packets sent through multilink are encapsulated as if Address and Control Field Compression and Protocol Field Compression were configured, with no async control character map, no Magic Number, no Link Quality Monitoring, no compound frames and no Self-Describing-Padding.
sections.eli5: Several small roads between two towns can be treated as one wide road. The towns only care about the combined road, not about which lane each truck used.

sections.title: Fragment Format
sections.content:
A network packet is first encapsulated by normal PPP rules, then broken into fragments sized for the member links. Implementations MUST NOT include the Address and Control fields in the material being fragmented. Each fragment is sent with the PPP protocol identifier 0x00-0x3d, followed by a multilink header. Small packets do not have to be fragmented, and fragments do not have to be equal in size. One suggested strategy is to divide packets in proportion to the speeds of the links.

The default header is four bytes: a Beginning bit, an Ending bit, 6 reserved bits that MUST be zero, and a 24-bit sequence number. After negotiation, a two-byte header is used instead, with 2 reserved bits and a 12-bit sequence number. The B bit is 1 on the first fragment of a PPP packet and the E bit is 1 on the last one. A fragment can have both set.

The sequence number is incremented for every fragment transmitted. There is no separate FCS for the reassembled packet; each fragment uses the FCS of the framing on its member link.

Systems that support multilink SHOULD implement Self-Describing-Padding from RFC 1570, and non-terminal fragments MUST NOT be padded by any other method.
sections.eli5: Cut a long letter into strips. On each strip you write whether it is the first strip, the last strip, and its number in the pile.

sections.title: The LCP Options
sections.content:
Multilink adds three LCP configuration options, covered in section 5 of the RFC.

The Multilink MRRU option (type 17, length 4) announces that the sender implements multilink and states the Maximum Receive Reconstructed Unit, the largest reassembled packet it accepts. A system MUST be able to receive a full 1500 octet Information field. The option MUST be included in every LCP negotiation that creates or joins a bundle, and a system MUST NOT send multilink packets on a link unless its peer offered the option and it was Configure-Acked.

The Short Sequence Number Header Format option (type 18, length 2) asks the peer to send fragments with 12-bit sequence numbers. If it is never negotiated, sequence numbers are 24 bits.

The Endpoint Discriminator option (type 19) identifies the system sending it, so a new link can be matched to an existing bundle. It carries a Class and an Address. Receiving this option alone does not mean multilink is requested. Joining a bundle securely needs a PPP authentication protocol, so a hostile peer cannot present a falsified discriminator.
sections.eli5: Before using the bags, both sides agree: we will number our papers, here is the biggest stack we can handle, and here is my name tag so you know it is me again.

sections.title: Joining a Bundle
sections.content:
When a new link arrives, the Endpoint Discriminator and authentication decide whether it joins an existing bundle or starts a new one. The RFC lists four cases:

  • No authentication and no discriminator: all new links MUST join one bundle, unless manual configuration says otherwise.
  • Discriminator only: a match MUST join the matching bundle, a mismatch MUST start a new bundle.
  • Authentication only: an authenticated match MUST join, a mismatch MUST start a new bundle.
  • Both: both must match to join; any mismatch starts a new bundle.

The Class field selects an address space. The values are 0 Null, 1 Locally Assigned Address, 2 IP Address, 3 IEEE 802.1 Globally Assigned MAC Address, 4 PPP Magic-Number Block and 5 Public Switched Network Directory Number. Classes with universally unique values are preferred. If the option is absent, the system MUST NOT Configure-Nak it and treats the peer as Class 0.

When a link Y is added to a bundle that has a single link X, a system MUST transmit a multilink-encapsulated packet on X before any on Y. The first fragment ever sent on a new bundle gets sequence number 0, and joining a link later does not reset the sequence space.
sections.eli5: When a new bag shows up, you check the name tag. If it matches a friend already in the group, it joins that group. If not, it starts a new one.

sections.title: Detecting Lost Fragments
sections.content:
Because links can be delayed differently, fragments can arrive out of order. On each member link the sender MUST send strictly increasing sequence numbers, and a number is used even for a fragment holding a whole packet. The receiver tracks the most recent sequence number on each link and takes the minimum over all links, called M.

A fragment is declared lost when M moves past the sequence number of an Ending fragment for a packet that has not been completely reassembled. The receiver then discards the fragments of the unfinished packets. The RFC mandates no procedure for detecting failed links, and suggests LCP echo-requests or link quality management.

Senders SHOULD avoid leaving member links idle, because M does not advance on an idle link. A sender can emit a null fragment, a multilink header with both B and E bits set and no payload, on a link that would otherwise go idle. Receivers SHOULD have a link idle timer to avoid indefinite stalls.

No amount of buffering is guaranteed to detect loss correctly, since an adversarial peer can withhold a fragment on one channel. A receiver that allocates less than S[1] + ... + S[N] + F[1] + ... + F[N] risks wrongly assuming loss, and SHOULD allocate at least twice that, where S is each channel's slippage and F its maximum fragment size.

If reliable operation is wanted, PPP Reliable Transmission MUST be negotiated on each member link first. Either way, an implementation MUST signal to the NCPs that a loss has occurred.
sections.eli5: You are counting papers as they come out of the bags. If you see paper 9 but paper 6 never showed up, and all the bags have moved past it, you decide paper 6 got lost and throw away the half-finished stack.

sections.title: Closing Links and Changes from RFC 1717
sections.content:
A member link is closed with the normal LCP Terminate-Request and Terminate-Ack. Closing one link does not end the procedure on the others, and the bundle's state persists while any member link is active. If only one link is left and the others closed gracefully, an implementation MAY stop using multilink headers.

Section 11 lists differences from RFC 1717. Using the Short Sequence Number option alone no longer signals multilink, the first sequence number after the virtual link opens must be 0, the MRRU has no default and must always be negotiated, Configure-Nak of the Endpoint Discriminator is forbidden, all links in a bundle must use the same sequence format, and several bundles may be manually configured when neither a discriminator nor authentication is used. Systems that follow the added restrictions interoperate with conforming RFC 1717 implementations.
sections.eli5: When one bag is put away the others keep going. The new rules mostly just tighten up the old ones so that everyone plays the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one sentence: operation of the protocol is no more and no less secure than operation of the PPP authentication protocols, and the reader is directed there. The practical consequence appears earlier, in the Endpoint Discriminator discussion: without authentication, a hostile peer could try to join an existing bundle with a falsified discriminator.
sections.eli5: The group is only as safe as the check you do at the door. Checking name tags alone is not enough if someone could fake a tag.

fields.name: B
fields.desc: Set to 1 on the first fragment of a PPP packet.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Set to 1 on the last fragment of a PPP packet.
